title: What a king is for
hookLine: Krishna answers: a king in Magadha holds kings captive, and a ruler's first duty is to protect
carry: raja dharma: a leader's first duty is to protect
last: KRISHNA, THE FRIEND WHO SEES FURTHER.

lines: YES. BUT THERE'S A KING IN MAGADHA.
cards: Krishna comes straight from Dwaraka, and Yudhishthira lays it all out. My father's wish. The sacrifice.
My ministers say yes, my brothers say yes. But you'll tell me the truth: should I perform the Rajasuya? And Krishna does.
You have every quality it takes, he says. Then comes the but. There's a king in Magadha.
While he lives, this can't be done.

teach.h: A SACRIFICE THAT MAKES A SOVEREIGN.
teach.b: First, what Yudhishthira is asking for. The Rajasuya is the great royal sacrifice, the one Harishchandra performed.
A king who completes it is honored by other kings as sovereign over them, so other rulers have to come, and bow, and bring gifts. That's exactly the problem Krishna names.
The king is Jarasandha of Magadha. Many kings already bow to him. Worse, he has captured kings in battle and holds them shut up in his mountain city, meaning to offer them as a sacrifice to Mahadeva.
While those kings sit in his prison, Krishna says, no one else can claim to be honored by the kings of the earth.
And Krishna tells it as someone hurt by it: fearing Jarasandha, his own people, the Yadavas, left Mathura for Dwaraka. Now look at what his counsel does. Yudhishthira asked, am I worthy of the honor?
Krishna answers, what about the people in that prison?

That's a teaching the epic comes back to again and again: raja dharma, the dharma of a king. In Hindu teaching, a ruler isn't there to be honored. He's there to protect, above all the ones who can't protect themselves.
Jarasandha is the picture of the opposite: a king who uses people, even as offerings.

teach.h: FIRST, SOMEONE HAS TO BE SET FREE.
teach.b: So before anyone can be honored, someone has to be set free. Many teachers read it as a question for anyone who leads, a family, a team, a class: whom are you protecting?
Tomorrow, Yudhishthira very nearly gives the whole thing up.

how: The Rajasuya belongs to the Vedic royal rites; in the Mahabharata, Yudhishthira's Rajasuya is the rite through which other kings recognize his rule at Indraprastha.

o: a sacrifice made to Mahadeva by a conquering king
a prison where a king keeps captured rulers
a royal rite where kings honor one king as sovereign

p: held to be offered to Mahadeva

s: Krishna told Yudhishthira to start the sacrifice at once
he said it couldn't be done while Jarasandha held kings captive.
in Hindu teaching, a king is there above all to protect
that's raja dharma, and Jarasandha, who uses kings as offerings, is its opposite.
Krishna claimed Jarasandha had never troubled his family
he said the Yadavas left Mathura for Dwaraka out of fear of Jarasandha.

games.q: you're Yudhishthira. Krishna says kings sit in Jarasandha's prison. as a king, what comes first?
o: being honored by the other kings.
freeing the ones who can't free themselves.
staying out of another king's business.
games.why: that's raja dharma: a ruler is there to protect. Krishna puts freeing the captives ahead of any honor.

practice: Bring to mind the people who depend on you in any way: a younger sibling, a friend, a team, a parent getting older. Name them one by one. If you pray, ask God to protect each one, and to help you protect them.
If you don't, hold each name for a breath and ask what looking out for them would mean this week.

wordCard.voice: The Rajasuya. The great royal sacrifice that makes a king sovereign over kings, and that Krishna says can't happen while Jarasandha holds kings captive.

orig.note: Sanskrit rājasūya: the royal sacrifice that consecrates a king as sovereign over other kings.

carryVoice: Your line: raja dharma, a leader's first duty is to protect. Before the honor, a prison door. Day seven hundred fifty-two, done.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, Rajasuyarambha Parva (Krishna's arrival and counsel; Jarasandha and the captive kings; the Yadavas leave Mathura)
Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Rajadharmanushasana Parva (Bhishma's teaching on the duties of kings, with protection foremost)
